narration: The first time you catch the thief, he looks surprised.
The second time, he runs.

The third time, he turns around before you even touch him.

“Seriously? We’re doing this again?”

Your hand freezes above your watch.

Because nobody is supposed to remember.

Three days earlier, your biggest problem was a sandwich.

You dropped it outside the café. Cheese down. Obviously.

You slapped your wrist against the table.

Clicked the little button on your old watch.

And the sandwich jumped off the pavement.

Back into your hand.

The café door closed. A cyclist rolled backward. Your coffee climbed back into its cup.

Then everything moved forward again.

You were holding lunch.

For about five seconds, you considered calling a scientist.
Then you ate the sandwich.

The rules took an afternoon to figure out.

One click sends the entire world back exactly thirty seconds.

Everything resets. Your position. Your pockets. Everyone’s conversations.

But you remember.

And the little light on the watch turns red.

It needs thirty seconds to recharge. Going backward doesn’t recharge it.
So you can repeat the same half-minute.
You can’t keep clicking your way back to last Tuesday.

Naturally, you use this extraordinary gift responsibly.

You throw a paper ball at a bin.

Miss.

Rewind.

Miss again.
Fourteen attempts later, you celebrate a shot nobody knows was difficult.

You try ordering coffee without saying “you too” when the cashier says, “Enjoy.”

Three attempts.

You ask someone out.

They say no.

You rewind and try a better opening.

They say no differently.

Apparently, time travel has limits.

By Monday, you’ve become unbearable.
You finish people’s sentences. Catch things without looking. Never lose at rock-paper-scissors.

Your little sister asks why you’re suddenly so annoying.

You rewind.

She asks again.

Some problems survive every timeline.

Then, outside the café, a man in a gray jacket takes a red backpack from an empty chair.

The owner is inside paying.

You’ve seen this moment before. He’s been watching that bag.

You grab his sleeve.

“Put it back.”

He shoves you. Coffee hits your shirt. He disappears around the corner.

Click.

The coffee returns to its cup.

The backpack returns to the chair.

This time, you block the corner.

He changes direction.

Strange.

Third attempt.

You wait beside the chair.

Before he reaches it, he looks straight at you.

“Seriously? We’re doing this again?”

You check the watch.

Red light.

Twenty-seven seconds until you can leave this conversation.

“You remember?”

He looks at your wrist.

Then back at your face.

“Oh,” he says. “It’s you.”

His name is Max.
Yesterday, he watched the same woman drop the same orange three times.

This morning, a bus arrived twice.

He thought he was having some kind of breakdown.

Then you grabbed his sleeve.

Twice.

You can turn back time.

Somehow, he stays awake through it.

You’ve spent three days believing your mistakes disappear.

For one other person, they don’t.
Look at him. He thinks every mistake disappears. But what if someone watching could see the futures he leaves behind?
What if each reset creates another branch? The same man, split across lives he will never remember.
In one future, he becomes a king. He has everything, except a way back.
In another, he dies. The world keeps moving. His story does not.
In one, he loses his home, his money, and everyone he knows.
In another, he becomes a boxer. He keeps winning, but every victory costs him something.
And in one, the thief kills him. The watch falls silent. There is no second chance.
What if those abandoned futures keep multiplying? What if every escape pushes time closer to collapse?
That is only a theory. But would he still press the button if he could see the cost?

You point at the backpack.

“Still stealing it?”

He smiles.

“Still stopping me?”

The light turns green.

Click.

Back beside the café.

You shout to the owner.

“Your bag!”

Max gets there first.

He points at you.

“That guy keeps trying to take it.”

Now the owner is holding your arm.

Max walks away laughing.

Thirty seconds.

Click.

You knock the backpack under the table.

Max kicks it out the other side.

Click.

You move the chair inside.

He waits by the door.

Click.

You know what he did last time.

He knows what you did last time.

Neither of you knows what the other will try next.
During the fifth attempt, a bus pulls up behind you.

Two police officers step off.

Finally.

You open your mouth.

But Max has already turned the corner.

The watch turns green.

You click.

And the officers step backward onto the bus.

The doors close.

The bus disappears.

You stare at the empty road.

You just sent help away.

Max notices your expression.

Then he notices the watch.

“That thing’s worth more than the bag.”

Now he comes toward you.
You run.

He catches your jacket.

You wait for green.

Click.

Back at the café.

He starts running immediately.

So do you.

For the first time, knowing the future doesn’t make you feel safe.

It means the man chasing you knows where you ran.

You reach the corner.

Stop.

The bus.

It arrives near the end of this half-minute.

Same road. Same stop. Same officers.

Max never saw them.

He was already around the corner.

You look at the watch.

Twenty seconds.

You could tell him about the police.

You could threaten him.

Instead, you glance down the alley.

Then at your wrist.

Max smiles.

He thinks you’re waiting to escape again.

You let him believe it.

Ten seconds.

You back toward the bus stop.

He follows.

Five.

An engine growls behind you.

The bus pulls in.

The doors open.

You step aside.

Two officers step down.

Max is still reaching for your wrist.

“This man took that backpack,” you say.

The owner runs out of the café.

“That’s him!”

Max looks at the officers.

Then at the green light.

He almost laughs.

“Fine. Go on, then.”

You understand what he’s waiting for.

Another attempt.

Another clean street.

Another chance to get away.

Your thumb rests on the button.

Then you lower your hand.

For once, the next thirty seconds belong to everybody.

Later, the owner buys you a coffee.

You knock it over.

Your hand moves toward your watch.

Across the table, he’s already reaching for napkins.

“Don’t worry,” he says. “Happens.”

You help him clean it up.

So, if you could rewind thirty seconds, what would you change first?

And who would you really hope couldn’t remember?
